children: By Samuel Indyk and Sophie  Kiderlin

Euro zone bond yields nudged lower on Thursday, reversing an earlier rise, as oil prices fell and UK gilts rallied sharply after the Bank of England said it would pause debt sales under its quantitative tightening programme.

The BoE left interest rates unchanged, as expected, while also setting out a long-term plan to offload its almost £500 billion ($670 billion) of bond holdings, which included a halt to sales until April and the end of sales of long-dated bonds entirely.
Britain's government bond yields fell sharply following the announcement, while yields on euro zone government bonds drifted lower.
The yield on the benchmark German 10-year government bond was last 3 basis points lower at 3.4817%, having nudged higher earlier in the day. It hit a 17-year peak of 3.5723% on Tuesday.
fell 2.6% on the day at $103.06 a barrel as reports of additional Saudi crude cargoes through Oman eased supply concerns.

Investors in Europe have been closely following high oil and gas prices, which have raised the risk that the European Central Bank will have to increase interest rates again, following last week's quarter-point hike.
"We would need to see a quick fall in energy prices to prevent another ECB hike," Jan von Gerich, chief analyst at Nordea, said.
Headline consumer prices rose 3.2% from a year ago in August, revised data from the EU statistics office Eurostat showed on Thursday, above the ECB's 2% target.
Markets are pricing in around a 40% chance of a rate hike from the ECB at its October meeting, while three quarter-point hikes are fully priced in by June of next year.
Germany's 2-year yield (DE2YT=RR), which is more sensitive to shifts in interest rate expectations, was last little changed on the day at 3.2096%, having retreated from the day's highs.

Short-dated euro zone government bond yields had climbed earlier in the session, the day after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in three years and signalled further increases to curb inflation.
"I think the message was clear that there's going to be more hiking," von Gerich said. "The message was on the hawkish side, there's no question about that."
The size and importance of the US economy and the influence of the Fed on other central banks mean US monetary policy tends to affect global bond markets.
